title: Marswalk hazard numbers
description: Numbers for the dust storm, radiation and low-oxygen events, the helmet HUD, the suit model and the route cost. Every value has a unit, a tag and a provenance block. Field definitions are in public/data/README.md.
historical_note: Every observation here is historical. None of it describes current conditions on Mars.

tags.DATA: Measured by a mission or a lab study, or stated in a NASA specification or procedure. The provenance block names the document and the page.
tags.DERIVED: Calculated by us from DATA values. The note gives the calculation.
tags.SIM: Our own assumption or game choice. The note says why and what it is based on.

provenance.license: Cited fact. The Mastcam-Z optical depth record (Lemmon, Mendeley Data) is CC BY 4.0.

provenance.reference: Marswalk team assumption
provenance.note: Time for the in-game optical depth to go from dust.tau.clear_season to dust.tau.storm_2022_peak. The real rise took up to one sol (dust.storm_2022.onset). #24 asks for 'a few minutes' so the event fits in an EVA.

provenance.reference: Marswalk team assumption, based on Sanchez-Lavega et al. 2025, JGR Planets 130, doi 10.1029/2024JE008565
provenance.locator: Section 6.6: storm A defined at Jezero by 'τ ≥ 1 between sols 417 and 472'
provenance.note: Above this optical depth the terrain-matching position fix is unavailable (plan section 4.2, issue #42). The 1.0 threshold is our choice. The paper uses τ ≥ 1 as its storm level at Jezero.

provenance.site: Jezero crater, view of a hill 36 km east
provenance.reference: Lemmon et al. 2022, Geophysical Research Letters 49, e2022GL100126
provenance.locator: Section 3.2: 'LOS opacity varied with column optical depth, peaking at 1.3 ± 0.1 per 10.5 km when the hill was only faintly visible'
provenance.note: Near-surface haze at the worst moment of the January 2022 storm at Jezero.

provenance.reference: Lemmon et al. 2022 (extinction) and Smith et al. 2019 (Koschmieder method, contrast threshold 0.02)
provenance.locator: Lemmon section 3.2; Smith et al. 2019 section 2
provenance.note: Extinction β = 1.3 / 10.5 km = 0.124 per km. Visibility V = -ln(0.02) / β = 3.912 / 0.124 = 31.6 km, rounded down. This fits the paper's hill at 36 km being 'only faintly visible'. A regional storm at Jezero cut visibility far less than the 2018 global storm at Gale (dust.visibility.gale_global_storm_2018).

provenance.reference: Smith et al. 2019, Visibility and Line-of-Sight Extinction Estimates in Gale Crater During the 2018/MY34 Global Dust Storm, Geophysical Research Letters 46, 9414-9421
provenance.locator: Plain language summary: 'At the peak of the storm, visibility was reduced to less than 3 km'
provenance.license: Cited fact. MSL images in PDS are public with no restriction of use.
provenance.note: Worst measured Mars surface visibility. Measured at Gale crater by Curiosity during a global storm, not at Jezero. Use only for a 'severe storm' scenario and say where it comes from.

provenance.reference: Smith et al. 2019, Geophysical Research Letters 46, 9414-9421
provenance.locator: Abstract: 'Peak extinction of > 1.1 km−1 was measured between sols 2086 and 2090'
provenance.note: Pair with dust.visibility.koschmieder_constant if the fog code wants an extinction coefficient instead of a distance.

provenance.reference: Smith et al. 2019, Geophysical Research Letters 46, 9414-9421
provenance.locator: Section 2: Koschmieder's law β = -ln(C_T)/D, 'For the average human eye under typical lab conditions, CT ≈ 0.02'
provenance.note: -ln(0.02) = 3.912. Visibility in km = 3.912 / extinction in km^-1.

provenance.sol_or_date: six Mars years of orbital records
provenance.reference: NASA/JPL, NASA Mars Orbiters Reveal Seasonal Dust Storm Pattern, 9 June 2016 (Kass et al. 2016, GRL, doi 10.1002/2016GL068978)
provenance.locator: Body text: 'Southern spring and summer have long been recognized as the dustiest part of the Martian year'
provenance.note: NASA gives the season in words. Ls 180-360 is the definition of southern spring and summer, not a number printed on the page. At Jezero, Sanchez-Lavega et al. 2025 put the dusty epoch at Ls 130-360.

provenance.site: Gale crater (-4.4 km MOLA), not Jezero
provenance.sol_or_date: 2012-08-07 to 2013-06-01 (first 300 sols, near solar maximum of cycle 24)
provenance.reference: Hassler et al. 2014, Mars' Surface Radiation Environment Measured with the Mars Science Laboratory's Curiosity Rover, Science 343, 1244797
provenance.locator: p. 1244797-3, text and Table 1: 'an average total GCR dose rate at Gale crater (– 4.4 km MOLA) of 0.210 ± 0.040 mGy/day'
provenance.license: Cited fact. RAD data in PDS are public with no restriction of use (NASA SPD-41A).
provenance.note: Background dose rate for the HUD (8.75 µGy per hour). Measured by Curiosity in Gale crater, not in Jezero. Jezero sits at about -2.4 km MOLA (terrain.json base_elev_m), about 2 km higher than Gale, so the thinner air above it would give a somewhat higher dose. No measurement at Jezero exists.

provenance.site: Gale crater (-4.4 km MOLA), not Jezero
provenance.reference: Hassler et al. 2014, Science 343, 1244797
provenance.locator: p. 1244797-3: 'an average GCR dose-equivalent rate on the Mars surface of 0.64 ± 0.12 millisieverts (mSv)/day'
provenance.note: Health-weighted dose (26.7 µSv per hour). Uses the measured mean quality factor 3.05 ± 0.3. Measured in Gale crater, not Jezero.

provenance.sol_or_date: first MSL Mars year, 2012-2014, extended by model over the solar cycle
provenance.reference: Guo et al. 2015, Modeling the Variations of Dose Rate Measured by RAD During the First MSL Martian Year: 2012-2014, Astrophysical Journal 810, 24
provenance.locator: arXiv 1507.03473v2 p. 20: 'The estimated surface dose equivalent rate ranges from about 0.35 mSv/day to about 1.15 mSv/day'
provenance.note: Tagged DERIVED because the authors fit a model to RAD data. The rate is highest at solar minimum and lowest at solar maximum.

provenance.product_id: NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 1 Rev B, requirement V1 4031

provenance.note: Shelter design target for a worst-case solar particle event.

provenance.reference: NASA CCMC Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information (DONKI)
provenance.locator: FLR record fields beginTime, peakTime, classType, sourceLocation; API https://ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/DONKI/WS/get/FLR?startDate=2017-09-10&endDate=2017-09-10
provenance.note: The flare that started the replayed event. DONKI links it to CME 2017-09-10T16:09:00-CME-001 (2650 km/s) and to SEP records 16:25Z (GOES-13 >100 MeV), 16:45Z (GOES-13 >10 MeV) and 20:00Z (SOHO COSTEP). All DONKI SEP records are near Earth. DONKI has no Mars SEP record.

provenance.reference: NASA CCMC DONKI notifications
provenance.locator: messageID 20170910-AL-001, messageIssueTime 2017-09-10T16:07Z
provenance.note: First DONKI alert, one minute after the flare peak.

provenance.reference: Zeitlin et al. 2018, Analysis of the Radiation Hazard Observed by RAD on the Surface of Mars During the September 2017 Solar Particle Event, Geophysical Research Letters 45, 5845-5851
provenance.locator: Section 3.1: 'A steady, statistically-significant increase in the E dose rate started around 19:50 UTC September 10'
provenance.note: The paper does not say whether this is time at Mars or time received on Earth. The difference is light travel time, about 10 to 20 minutes.

provenance.site: Sun to Gale crater, not Jezero
provenance.reference: DONKI flare record and Zeitlin et al. 2018
provenance.locator: Flare peakTime 16:06Z; Zeitlin section 3.1 onset 19:50Z
provenance.note: 19:50Z minus 16:06Z = 3 h 44 min. That is the real warning a crew at Gale would have had from the flare to the first dose rise. Zeitlin says the event was 'unambiguously underway by about 21:00 UTC', 4 h 54 min after the flare peak.

provenance.instrument: RAD (B detector, silicon converted to water)
provenance.reference: Zeitlin et al. 2018, Geophysical Research Letters 45, 5845-5851
provenance.locator: Table 1, 'Average rates, 5 days pre-SPE', B omnidirectional
provenance.note: Background level just before the event. It is close to Hassler's long-term 210 µGy/day. The E detector, behind more shielding, read 265.

provenance.reference: Zeitlin et al. 2018, Geophysical Research Letters 45, 5845-5851
provenance.locator: Table 1, 'Peak rate', B omnidirectional; section 3.1 'The event peaked on September 11, from about 4:00 to 14:00 UTC'
provenance.note: About 3 times background, or 29.9 µGy per hour. The E detector peaked at 588 µGy/day. The B dose equivalent peak was 841 µSv/day.

provenance.sol_or_date: 5 days after the shock arrival, 2017-09-13 onward
provenance.reference: Zeitlin et al. 2018, Geophysical Research Letters 45, 5845-5851
provenance.locator: Table 1, 'Average rates, 5 days post-SPE', B omnidirectional
provenance.note: Below the pre-event level. The shock front swept away part of the galactic cosmic rays (a Forbush decrease).

provenance.reference: Zeitlin et al. 2018, Geophysical Research Letters 45, 5845-5851
provenance.locator: Section 3.1: 'the SPE contributed 544 µGy of dose in water as measured by the B detector, and 369 µGy of dose as measured by E'
provenance.note: Whole event, from onset to shock arrival. Zeitlin: staying outside for the whole event 'would have been comparable to adding about two days of GCR exposure'. This event is a timing hazard, not a lethal dose.

provenance.reference: Zeitlin et al. 2018, Geophysical Research Letters 45, 5845-5851
provenance.locator: Section 3.1: 'unambiguously underway by about 21:00 UTC on 10 September, and dose rates doubled within about 7 hours'
provenance.note: How fast the dose rate climbs after onset.

provenance.reference: Zeitlin et al. 2018, Geophysical Research Letters 45, 5845-5851
provenance.locator: Section 3.1: onset 19:50 UTC 10 Sep; 'Dose rates then fell gradually until about 05:00 UTC September 13, at which point they fell steeply'
provenance.note: Onset to shock arrival is 57 h 10 min. The profile is in models.sep_2017_profile.

provenance.reference: NASA, NASA Watches Mars Light Up During Epic Solar Storm, updated 10 June 2024
provenance.locator: Body text: astronauts next to Curiosity 'would have received a radiation dose of 8,100 micrograys'
provenance.note: Reference only, not replayed. Largest event RAD had measured by 2024, after an X12 flare on the far side of the Sun. NASA gives no peak rate or duration, and particles reached Mars 'in just tens of minutes'. DONKI has no SEP or flare record for it (SEP query for 2024-05-15 to 2024-05-25 returns an empty list), which shows that Earth-side monitoring alone can miss an event at Mars.

provenance.reference: Marswalk team choice
provenance.note: The simulated suit uses NASA's Exploration EMU (xEMU) consumables, the only suit with every number confirmed in NASA documents. The xEMU was designed for the Moon. Ogilvie et al. 2026 (ICES-2026-127) say it 'would not be feasible to operate on the surface on Mars' (p. 1), mainly because it weighs 177 kg (p. 5). The simulator uses its consumables but not its mass (see metabolic.model_mass).

provenance.reference: NASA JSC, Schematics and Behavioral Description for the AEMU PLSS, CTSD-ADV-959 Rev A
provenance.locator: p. 13: 'The POV stores ~1.7 lbm of usable oxygen'; charged to 3000 psia at 60 °F
provenance.note: 771 g = 1.7 x 453.592 g. At the xEMU design average of 1200 BTU/hr, an 8 h EVA uses 693 g (see suit.o2.design_eva_use), so the tank fits the spec with about 10 % margin.

provenance.reference: NASA JSC, CTSD-ADV-959 Rev A
provenance.locator: p. 13: 'The SOV stores ~1.7 lbm of usable oxygen'
provenance.note: Emergency supply. It runs in open-loop purge mode, so it lasts far less time than the primary (suit.o2.secondary_abort_time).

provenance.reference: NASA JSC, CTSD-ADV-959 Rev A
provenance.locator: p. 15: 'the SPV would offer the 30 minute abort time at the higher flow rate'
provenance.note: Time to get back to shelter on the secondary oxygen in high-flow purge. Lower-flow configurations last longer: the xEVA con ops (EVA-EXP-0042 Rev B, p. 36) gives 'an additional 1 hour of secondary/backup O2'.

provenance.reference: NASA, Exploration EVA System Concept of Operations, EVA-EXP-0042 Rev B
provenance.locator: Section 4.1.4: 'The xEVA suit will support EVAs of up to 8 hours in duration (6±2 hours)'
provenance.note: Nominal EVA is 6 h, maximum 8 h.

provenance.reference: NASA, Exploration EVA System Concept of Operations, EVA-EXP-0042 Rev B
provenance.locator: p. 36: 'Suit pressures range from 0.4 psid to 8.2 psid, with a nominal EVA pressure of 4.3 psid'
provenance.note: Same 4.3 psi as the mockups and the ISS EMU. 29.6 kPa = 4.3 x 6.895.

provenance.instrument: xEMU PLSS battery BATT-690 (Li-ion, LG MJ1 18650 cells, 8S-8P)
provenance.reference: NASA JSC, CTSD-ADV-959 Rev A
provenance.locator: p. 18, battery table: 'BATT-690 Primary PLSS Battery 29.1 ... 8S – 8P 756'
provenance.note: Nominal 29.1 V. The schematic on p. 8 of the same document labels it '28V Nom/~900Wh'. We use the table value. The suit also has a 95 Wh auxiliary thermal loop battery and a 189 Wh accessory battery, not modelled.

provenance.product_id: CTSD-ADV-959 Rev A; EVA-EXP-0042 Rev B
provenance.reference: suit.battery.primary_capacity and suit.eva_duration_max
provenance.locator: 756 Wh (p. 18) over 8 h (con ops section 4.1.4)
provenance.note: 756 Wh / 8 h = 94.5 W, assuming the battery is sized to last exactly the maximum EVA. No NASA document we found states the measured average draw.

suit.battery.effort_share.unit: fraction of battery draw that scales with metabolic rate
suit.battery.effort_share.label: SIM

provenance.reference: Marswalk team assumption
provenance.note: #19 wants battery use to follow effort. Battery W = 94.5 x (0.7 + 0.3 x metabolic W / 352). At the design average (352 W) this gives 94.5 W. At 589 W (flat walking at 1 m/s) it gives 113 W. The idea: fans, pumps and cooling work harder with more body heat, while radio, displays and sensors do not. The 30 % split is our guess. No source gives it.

provenance.product_id: CTSD-ADV-780 Rev B (xEMU PLSS specification), cited by ICES-2026-127
provenance.reference: Ogilvie et al. 2026, Mars Spacesuit Mass Requirements, ICES-2026-127
provenance.locator: p. 4: 'the metabolic average rate for exploration suit sizing is currently at 1200 BTU/hr (352 Watts)'
provenance.note: The rate the consumables are sized for. The paper adds that Mars rates are expected to be higher because of the higher gravity.

provenance.product_id: CTSD-ADV-780 Rev B, cited by ICES-2026-127
provenance.reference: Ogilvie et al. 2026, ICES-2026-127
provenance.locator: p. 4: 'The xEMU specifications require a short duration capability to manage a 3000 BTU/hr peak rate for 10 minutes'
provenance.note: Suit cooling limit. A walking rate above this for more than 10 minutes is beyond the suit spec. The HUD can warn on it.

provenance.reference: suit.metabolic.design_average, metabolic.energy_per_litre_o2, metabolic.o2_density
provenance.note: 352 W x 8 h x 3600 s / 20900 J/L = 485 L O2 x 1.429 g/L = 693 g. Check that the model is consistent with the 771 g tank.

suit.reserve.time.unit: min at the current metabolic rate
suit.reserve.time.label: Apollo 17 procedures · NASA

provenance.product_id: Apollo 17 Final Lunar Surface Procedures, Vol. 2 Contingency
provenance.reference: NASA MSC, Apollo 17 Final Lunar Surface Procedures, Volume 2: Contingency
provenance.locator: Tables 2.4-2 and 2.4-3, printed pp. 16-17: '30 MINUTES RESERVES MAINTAINED ON ALL PLSS CONSUMABLES AT STATION METABOLIC RATE'
provenance.note: The reserve for the low-oxygen rule in #26. The ISS EMU uses the same 30 minutes (Moore 2014, NTRS 20140009556, slide 11: '30 minutes for reserve').

suit.reserve.walkback_pad.unit: % added to walking metabolic rate for the walkback estimate
suit.reserve.walkback_pad.label: Apollo 15 planning · NASA

provenance.reference: Benjamin, Apollo 15 EVA Capability and Constraints Envelopes, Bellcomm memorandum B70 10028
provenance.locator: p. 1: 'A 20% pad is required for emergency walkback, making the metabolic rate 1440 BTU/hr at a speed of 3.3 km/hr'
provenance.note: Walkback O2 = (walking O2 rate along the route home) x 1.2. Apollo used this pad together with the 30 min reserve.

provenance.reference: Marswalk team assumption
provenance.note: Margin = O2 time left - (walkback time with the 20 % pad + 30 min reserve). Caution when the margin falls below 15 min, warning when it reaches 0 (#26). The 15 min is our choice, so the caution shows several minutes of walking before the warning.

provenance.reference: Marswalk team assumption, following the Apollo reserve rule
provenance.note: Warning when the margin defined in suit.alert.caution_margin reaches zero, so the crew has only the 30 min reserve left beyond the walk home.

metabolic.minetti_polynomial.unit: coefficients of i^5..i^0, Cw in J per kg body mass per m, i = gradient (rise/run), 1 g
metabolic.minetti_polynomial.label: Minetti et al. 2002

provenance.reference: Minetti AE, Moia C, Roi GS, Susta D, Ferretti G 2002, Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes, J Appl Physiol 93:1039-1046
provenance.note: Net cost (measured minus resting), valid for i = -0.45 to +0.45. The polynomial reads 2.5 at i = 0, but the measured level value is 1.64. That is why the suit model uses Table 2 (metabolic.minetti_table) instead. A lab study, not NASA data.

metabolic.minetti_table.unit: [gradient i, Cw in J per kg body mass per m], net, 1 g
metabolic.minetti_table.label: Minetti et al. 2002

provenance.reference: Minetti et al. 2002, J Appl Physiol 93:1039-1046
provenance.locator: Table 2, minimum Cw at each gradient; abstract: 'The minimum Cw was 1.64 ± 0.50 J·kg−1·m−1 at a 1.0 ± 0.3 m/s speed on the level'
provenance.note: Measured walking cost at each gradient. Interpolate linearly. Clamp i to [-0.45, 0.45]. A 20 deg slope is i = tan 20 deg = 0.364.

provenance.reference: Minetti et al. 2002, J Appl Physiol 93:1039-1046
provenance.locator: Methods, p. 1040: 'assuming an energy equivalent of 20.9 kJ/l O2 (corresponding to a nonproteic respiratory exchange ratio of 0.96)'
provenance.note: 4.99 kcal per litre. NASA uses the same round number: Paul 2012 (NTRS 20120003917) says 'approximately 5 kcal of energy must be liberated to consume 1 liter of oxygen'.

provenance.product_id: NIST Chemistry WebBook SRD 69, oxygen C7782447
provenance.reference: NIST Chemistry WebBook, Thermophysical Properties of Fluid Systems, oxygen
provenance.locator: Isobaric table at 0.101325 MPa: row 273.150 K, density 1.42903 kg/m3
provenance.note: Converts litres of O2 (standard conditions) to grams.

provenance.instrument: PLSS O2 pressure decay, LCG heat balance, heart rate
provenance.reference: Waligora JM, Horrigan DJ 1975, Metabolism and Heat Dissipation During Apollo EVA Periods, in Biomedical Results of Apollo, NASA SP-368
provenance.locator: Table 2, 'All activities' mean: 980 (234) kJ/h (kcal/h), 158.74 h
provenance.note: 234 kcal/h, 930 BTU/h, about 67 g O2 per hour. Plausibility check for the suit model. Rates by task in the same table: ALSEP deployment 1018 kJ/h, geology stations 1018, overhead 1123, rover riding 518.

provenance.instrument: PLSS O2 pressure decay, LCG heat balance
provenance.reference: Waligora and Horrigan 1975, NASA SP-368 ch. 4
provenance.locator: Table 2, 'Rover riding' mean: 518 (123) kJ/h (kcal/h), 25.28 h
provenance.note: Lowest measured EVA activity. The suit model uses it as the metabolic rate of a suited astronaut standing still (the 'base' term). Using it for standing is our assumption: the number itself is measured, but it was measured while riding the rover.

provenance.instrument: PLSS O2 pressure decay, LCG heat balance
provenance.reference: Waligora and Horrigan 1975, NASA SP-368 ch. 4
provenance.locator: Table 4, 'Metabolic Analyses of Apollo 14 EVA Traverses', p. 125, row 'Totals, LM to LM'
provenance.note: The best walking-only data from the Moon: about 500 to 530 kJ per km at 1/6 g. Up the +5.0 % leg (1547 m) the crew slowed to 1.86 km/h, and down the -6.4 % leg they sped up to 3.82 km/h with similar metabolic rates. The authors saw 'a very poor correlation between traverse rate and metabolic rate'. The crew held a steady effort and let speed change, which is the basis of mobility.speed_rule.

metabolic.hr_fit.unit: MR (BTU/hr) = intercept + slope x HR (beats per minute)
metabolic.hr_fit.label: Shuttle/ISS EVA · NASA

provenance.instrument: EMU PLSS O2 decay, heart rate
provenance.reference: Hoffmann B 2021, Extravehicular Activity Metabolic Rate Model: Metabolic Rate Estimated from Heart Rate (chapter 5)
provenance.locator: Table 5.1, coefficient tests: 'Intercept 284.55 ... Slope 5.984'
provenance.note: For a HUD heart-rate readout. It turns a simulated metabolic rate into a heart rate: HR = (MR - 284.55) / 5.984. R2 is only 0.402 across crew members, so treat the heart rate shown as illustrative. Fitted to microgravity EVAs, not walking.

metabolic.mars_suited_transport_cost.unit: [speed m/s, mL O2 per kg body mass per km], gross, 3/8 g, suited
metabolic.mars_suited_transport_cost.label: EVA Walkback Test · NASA JSC

provenance.instrument: Mark III suit (121 kg total suit weight as listed), partial gravity simulator, treadmill
provenance.site: NASA JSC, simulated Mars gravity (3/8 g)
provenance.reference: Norcross J et al. 2008, Feasibility of Suited 10 km Walkback on the Moon, AsMA presentation
provenance.locator: Slide 12, 'Energy-Velocity Series Results - Mars', Transport Cost chart, 'Mars, suited' fit line at 2.4 mph and 3.4 mph
provenance.note: The only suited walking data at Mars gravity we found. Values were read from a chart (about ±5 %). They match the metabolic cost chart on the same slide (about 22 mL/kg/min at 2.4 mph and 41 at 3.4 mph). Unsuited Mars walking at the same speeds costs about 130 to 150 mL/kg/km. The slides conclude the Mark III 'was extremely limited on Mars'. Subjects averaged 81.4 ± 7.8 kg (slide 4).

metabolic.ist2_grade_gravity_delta.unit: [grade, rise in VO2 in mL per kg body mass per min going from 0.12 g to 0.32 g], suited

provenance.instrument: Mark III suit at 29.6 kPa, treadmill, partial gravity offload
provenance.reference: Norcross JR et al. 2010, Metabolic Costs and Biomechanics of Inclined Ambulation and Exploration Tasks in a Planetary Suit, NASA/TP-2010-216125
provenance.locator: Results, text with Fig. 36: 'as the grade increased to 20% and 30%, this difference increased to 8.7 and 17.0 mL•kg-1•min-1'
provenance.note: Gravity barely matters on the flat but matters a lot uphill. Used to calibrate metabolic.grade_factor. Speeds were 0.56 to 0.97 m/s.

metabolic.farley_reduced_gravity_walking.unit: % drop in walking metabolic rate when gravity is reduced by 75 %
metabolic.farley_reduced_gravity_walking.label: Farley and McMahon 1992

provenance.reference: Farley CT, McMahon TA 1992, Energetics of walking and running: insights from simulated reduced-gravity experiments, J Appl Physiol 73:2709-2712
provenance.locator: Abstract: 'When gravity is reduced by 75%, the rate of energy consumption is reduced by 72% during running but only by 33% during walking'
provenance.note: Why the model does not scale the level walking cost by g. Only the abstract was available. The values at 0.5 g and 0.75 g are in the paywalled full text.

metabolic.grade_factor.unit: multiplier on the gravity-scaled grade term
metabolic.grade_factor.label: DERIVED · NASA IST-2

provenance.reference: Calibration of Minetti Table 2 against metabolic.ist2_grade_gravity_delta
provenance.locator: Fig. 36 and text
provenance.note: With a factor of 1.0, Minetti's grade cost scaled by g predicts a 7.8 to 13.5 mL/kg/min rise at 30 % grade for 0.12 to 0.32 g. IST-2 measured 17.0. 1.3 matches the middle of the IST-2 speed range. The per-subject speeds are not published, so anything from 1.06 to 1.6 fits. The suit makes climbing costlier than unsuited walking.

provenance.reference: Norcross J et al. 2008, Feasibility of Suited 10 km Walkback on the Moon, AsMA presentation
provenance.locator: Slide 4, subjects: 'Body Mass (kg) 81.4 ± 7.8'; slide 5, hardware: '121 kg total suit weight'
provenance.note: Default astronaut plus suit mass. It is the configuration the level cost was measured with, so the model stays inside its data. The xEMU weighs 177 kg (391 lbm, Ogilvie et al. 2026, p. 5). Putting it in M raises every cost by 27 %. Ogilvie et al. say a Mars suit must be lighter than that.

provenance.instrument: Mark III suit, treadmill at 3/8 g
provenance.reference: Norcross J et al. 2008, Feasibility of Suited 10 km Walkback on the Moon, AsMA presentation
provenance.locator: Slide 12, 'Mars, suited' data range, 2.4 to 3.4 mph

provenance.reference: NASA, Exploration EVA System Concept of Operations, EVA-EXP-0042 Rev B
provenance.locator: p. 40: 'Traverses assume an ~2 km/hr walking pace over relatively level regolith'
provenance.note: NASA's conservative planning pace. It is used to set the 2 km walking radius around the lander. It does not account for slope or obstacles.

provenance.reference: Benjamin, Apollo 15 EVA Capability and Constraints Envelopes, Bellcomm B70 10028
provenance.locator: p. 1: 'The metabolic rate for planned walking traverses is 1200 BTU/hr at a speed of 3.3 km/hr'

provenance.instrument: Mark III suit, treadmill at 1/6 g
provenance.reference: Norcross J et al. 2009, Feasibility of Performing a Suited 10-km Ambulation on the Moon, NASA/TP-2009-214796
provenance.locator: p. 28: 'The mean time to complete the 10 km was 96 minutes, at an average velocity of 1.74 ms-1 (3.9 mph)'
provenance.note: Fastest sustained suited walk. Lunar gravity on a level treadmill, so it is an upper bound and too fast for Mars.

provenance.reference: Marswalk team assumption
provenance.note: Default walking speed on flat ground, the value the engine already uses. It lies between Apollo's planning walkback speed (0.92 m/s) and the slowest suited speed tested at Mars gravity (1.07 m/s). Flat walking at this speed costs 589 W in the suit model, already 1.7 times the xEMU design average.

provenance.reference: Marswalk team assumption, capped by mobility.speed.mars_suited_tested
provenance.note: Top speed when the player hurries. Close to the fastest suited speed tested at Mars gravity (1.52 m/s). The suit model is valid up to there. Flat at 1.5 m/s costs 1138 W (3884 BTU/hr), above the suit's 10 min cooling peak (suit.metabolic.design_peak).

provenance.reference: Marswalk team assumption
provenance.note: Floor for mobility.speed_rule on steep climbs, so a 20 deg slope stays walkable instead of stalling. 0.3 m/s is our choice.

provenance.reference: Marswalk team assumption, based on Waligora and Horrigan 1975 (metabolic.apollo14_traverse)
provenance.locator: Table 4 and text: crews 'maintained a comfortable walking effort'
provenance.note: On a slope, the walker keeps the metabolic power of flat walking at mobility.speed.flat (589 W) and the speed changes to match. Solve models.walking_metabolic for v, then clamp to [mobility.speed.min, mobility.speed.jog]. Results with the default mass: +5 deg 0.63 m/s, +10 deg 0.44, +15 deg 0.34, +20 deg 0.30 (at the floor), -5 deg 1.12, -10 deg 1.09, -20 deg 0.79. Apollo 14 crews did the same: 1.86 km/h up 5 % and 3.82 km/h down 6.4 %. No NASA source gives suited speed as a function of slope.

provenance.reference: NASA, Exploration EVA System Concept of Operations, EVA-EXP-0042 Rev B
provenance.locator: p. 38: 'Walking up/down/across a slope of up to 20° [Note: Apollo 15 traversed on slopes of ~17°]'
provenance.note: NASA's suited walking limit. The 2025 Artemis overview (NTRS 20250009323, p. 21) gives the same 'Surface slope limit for EVA (2km): <20 deg'. The engine still uses 25 deg (docs/marswalk-assets/testbench-reference). 25 deg only matches the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle's climbing spec (NASA TM X-64623, p. 6: 'Climbing a 25-deg slope fully loaded'), a vehicle limit. A route issue should move the engine to 20.

provenance.reference: Marswalk team assumption, between Norcross et al. 2010 and the xEVA 20 deg limit
provenance.locator: NASA/TP-2010-216125 p. 98: 'metabolic rate differences became most significant at steeper grades (≥ 20%)'
provenance.note: The engine's current caution threshold. No NASA source states 15 deg. It sits between 11.3 deg (20 % grade, where Norcross saw the cost of climbing in a suit become significant) and the 20 deg suited limit. Apollo 15 walked slopes of about 17 deg.

walking_metabolic.label: DERIVED · Minetti 2002 + NASA suited data
walking_metabolic.description: Metabolic power and O2 use of a suited astronaut walking at speed v on gradient i at Mars gravity. For #19 (suit model) and #41 (per-leg O2).

inputs.v: walking speed along the ground, m/s
inputs.i: gradient, rise over run (tan of slope angle). Positive uphill
inputs.M: astronaut plus suit mass, kg. Default metabolic.model_mass.total_kg = 202.4

C_L0.unit: J per kg total mass per m

C_Lv.unit: J per kg per m, per m/s above v0

formula: Cw(i) = linear interpolation of metabolic.minetti_table at clamp(i, -0.45, 0.45)
C_level(v) = C_L0 + C_Lv * max(0, v - v0)
VO2 = P / J_per_L * 60                    (L O2 per min)
O2_rate = VO2 * rho_O2                    (g O2 per min)
O2 for a leg = sum over segments of P * (segment length / v) / J_per_L * rho_O2   (g)
assumptions: DERIVED: C_L0 and C_Lv make the formula reproduce the EVA Walkback Test transport costs for suited walking at 3/8 g: 340 mL/kg_body/km at 1.07 m/s and 450 at 1.52 m/s. For each speed, C = cost x 20.9 J/mL x 81.4 kg / 202.4 kg - P_base / (M v). Below 1.07 m/s the level cost is held at C_L0. No suited Mars data exist there.
SIM: the level term does not scale with g. Farley and McMahon found walking cost falls only 33 % for a 75 % drop in gravity, and the Walkback Test level cost was already measured at 3/8 g.

DERIVED: the grade term is Minetti's 1 g cost above level, scaled linearly by g / g_earth, because climbing work is m g h. Minetti's 24 % efficiency above +15 % gradient supports that. K_grade = 1.3 calibrates it to suited IST-2 data.
SIM: downhill uses Minetti's negative grade cost scaled the same way. No suited downhill data were found. P_walk never goes below zero.
SIM: P_base (144 W) is the Apollo rover-riding rate, used for a suited astronaut standing still.
SIM: valid for 0.3 to 1.52 m/s and slopes up to 20 deg (i = 0.364). Outside that it extrapolates.

checks.versus_apollo: Apollo lunar EVAs averaged 272 W (67 g O2 per hour). Flat walking here is 589 W (144 g per hour). The 2.2x difference matches the Walkback Test finding that suited walking at 3/8 g costs far more than at 1/6 g. On the Moon, Apollo 14 walking cost about 500 to 530 kJ per km. Here it is 589 kJ per km at more than twice the gravity.
checks.versus_tank: One flat km uses 40 g, 5 % of the 771 g xEMU primary O2. The 20 deg climb uses 129 to 142 g, 17 to 18 %. Walking nonstop on flat ground would empty the tank in about 19 km, or 5.3 h.

sep_2017_profile.label: RAD · Curiosity · Gale
sep_2017_profile.description: Dose rate keypoints of the 10-13 September 2017 solar particle event, measured by RAD in Gale crater (B detector, water), for #25. Times are hours after the flare peak (2017-09-10T16:06Z). #25 compresses the timeline to fit an EVA, and the compression factor is a game choice (SIM).
sep_2017_profile.unit: t_h: hours after flare peak; rate: µGy/day (water)

points.note: Flare peak. Background, 5-day mean before the event (Zeitlin Table 1)
03:00Z 11 Sep: 'about 90% of the eventual peak' (Zeitlin section 3.1), 0.9 x 718
05:00Z 13 Sep, just before the shock. The paper says rates 'fell gradually' to here, with no value. 245 = 208 / 0.85, so the 15 % drop lands on the measured post-event mean
Shock arrival: 'a sudden drop of about 15%', then the 5-day post-event mean of 208 (Zeitlin Table 1)

provenance.reference: Zeitlin et al. 2018, Geophysical Research Letters 45, 5845-5851; flare time from DONKI 2017-09-10T15:35:00-FLR-001
provenance.locator: Section 3.1 and Table 1
provenance.license: Cited facts. RAD data in PDS are public with no restriction of use (NASA SPD-41A).
provenance.note: Interpolate linearly between points. The full-resolution curve is in the RAD PDS archive (directory SOL_01773_01869). Extracting it belongs to #31.
